title: Light affliction (2 Corinthians 4:16–18)
hook: outwardly wasting, inwardly renewed day by day

segments.voice: Yesterday, clay jars: treasure in earthen vessels. Your line was pressed, not crushed. Did you catch yourself saying it over a cup? Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

Light. That's the word Paul uses for his troubles. Light. This is the same man whose list we read two days ago: beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, lowered from a city wall in a basket. Later in this very letter he'll write that list down. And here, a few verses after the clay jars, he calls it all light affliction. A friend who said that about a year like that might get a worried phone call. So either Paul is in denial, or he's weighing his troubles against something so heavy that they really do feel light. Today: light affliction.

Here are the lines, in the King James words: "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Two people in one body. The outward one is wearing out. Paul doesn't hide that. Knees, eyes, energy, the face in the mirror. The inward one is being made new. And not once. Day by day. Then the weighing: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." Hear it as a balance scale. On one side, the affliction: real, but light, and only for a moment. On the other side, glory: a weight, and eternal. Paul isn't saying the suffering is small. He's saying it's small next to what it sits beside. Then the last line tells you where to look: "the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." Temporal means for a time. The hospital bracelet, the bills, the gray hair, all of that is real, and all of it is for a time. Some readers hear a promise about the life to come; some also hear something that happens now, a little each day: an inner life that keeps being renewed while the outer one tires. And notice the words day by day. Not a single dramatic rescue. Just today, and then today again.

Here's the practice: renew yourself today. Settle, and breathe. Notice your outward self first, without judging it: whatever aches, whatever's tired. Let it be tired. Then turn inward. Ask what would make the inner person a little newer today. Not a whole new life. One small thing: a short walk outside, a psalm read slowly, a call to someone who makes you laugh, an early night. Choose one. If you pray, you can ask God for today's renewal, just today's. The bell holds the time.
Light affliction. Paul's name for real suffering, weighed against an eternal weight of glory, while the inward self is renewed day by day.
Your line: renewed day by day. Today, do the one small renewing thing you chose, and tonight, notice whether the inside feels a little newer. Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians read 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 at funerals, in hospitals and in seasons of aging or illness, as words about an inner life renewed while the body wears out, and about a hope beyond what is seen.

fork.setup: you're Paul, writing to Corinth. you've just admitted that your outward man is perishing. what do you write next?
options: so we give up, and wait for the end.
yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
so we must guard the body above all.
fork.reveal: "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." he names the wearing out, and doesn't stop there.

original.note: Greek: is being renewed, made new again, in 2 Corinthians 4:16.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul says suffering doesn't really matter.
what it means: real suffering, weighed against an eternal weight of glory, while the inner self is renewed day by day.
what a scholar hears: a scale with light and moment on one side, weight and eternal on the other; and the renewal is day by day, not once.

notes: 'Day by day' is said to read, word for word, 'day and day' (Greek ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ in 4:16); attributed to 'some readers'. Keeper to confirm the Greek.
Greek ἀνακαινοῦται (4:16); confirm accent and pronunciation guide.

The balance-scale picture (light vs weight) is the writer's image for Paul's contrast, not something the text states. Deliberately left out: any claim that Hebrew 'kavod' (glory) means 'weight', as an etymology the text doesn't give.
The hook links 4:17 to the hardship list in chapter 11 ('later in this very letter'); confirm that framing.
howItsDone names funerals and hospitals as settings; Keeper to confirm.
